Accepted at the Gen2Workshop at ICLR 2026 (Tiny Papers Track)
CONTINUOUSDIFFUSIONTRANSFORMERS FORDE-
SIGNINGSYNTHETICREGULATORYELEMENTS
Jonathan Liu∗& Kia Ghods∗
Department of Computer Science
Princeton University
{jonathanliu,kia.ghods}@princeton.edu
ABSTRACT
We present a parameter-efficient Diffusion Transformer (DiT) for generating
200 bp cell-type-specific regulatory DNA sequences. By replacing the U-Net
backbone of DNA-Diffusion (DaSilva et al., 2025) with a transformer denoiser
equipped with a 2D CNN input encoder, our model matches the U-Net’s best val-
idation loss in 13 epochs (60×fewer) and converges 39% lower, while reducing
memorization from 5.3% to 1.7% of generated sequences aligning to training data
via BLAT. Ablations show the CNN encoder is essential: without it, validation
loss increases 70% regardless of positional embedding choice. We further apply
DDPO finetuning using Enformer as a reward model, achieving a 38×improve-
ment in predicted regulatory activity. Cross-validation against DRAKES on an
independent prediction task confirms that improvements reflect genuine regula-
tory signal rather than reward model overfitting.
1 INTRODUCTION
The ability to generate short DNA sequences with designated regulatory effects remains a bottleneck
for safe and precise genetic modulation. Existing approaches broadly fall into (1) DNA foundation
models and (2) small-insert, objective-driven generators (often diffusion-based). While transform-
ers have achieved strong performance in sequence modeling, conditioning and controllability for
regulatory design remain challenging.
Specifically, we use a Diffusion Transformer to learn the diffusion process (Peebles & Xie, 2023).
We choose a transformer model because U-nets—which have fixed receptive fields—fail to model
long-distance DNA interactions. Works in the literature have not trained diffusion models to gen-
erate short-inserts that optimize regulatory activity, however, our lightweight models allow us to
conduct normally expensive rollouts during RL finetuning. As a result, our final model is capable of
returning DNA segments that natively have high predicted promoter activity and DNA accessibility.
We make the following contributions: (1)Continuous DiT for regulatory design:We develop
a parameter-efficient transformer-based diffusion model for generating synthetic 200 bp regulatory
elements under cell-type-specific objectives that surpasses the performance of previous models in
60x fewer steps and with 6x fewer parameters; and (2)Post-training with RL optimization:We
perform RLVR-style finetuning using Enformer as a reward model to improve accessibility/activity
proxies. Using DRAKES as a verifier, we find that our RL provides signal to similar tasks (Wang
et al., 2024).
2 RELATEDWORKS
Deep learning for regulatory genomics advanced throughsequence-to-functionpredictors such as
DeepSEA (Zhou & Troyanskaya, 2015), Basset (Kelley et al., 2016), Basenji (Kelley et al., 2018),
BPNet (Avsec et al., 2021b), and Enformer (Avsec et al., 2021a). We use Enformer (cell-type-
specific CAGE/DNase from 196kb context) as an evaluation oracle. These predictors naturally in-
duce an inverse problem: can wedesignsequences that achieve desired regulatory behaviors?
∗Equal Contribution

Generative approaches fall into two regimes: (1) largeDNA foundation models(autoregressive or
masked) that capture broad genomic structure, and (2)small-insert, objective-driven generators
that produce short cis-regulatory candidates conditioned on cell type and assay objectives. DNA-
Diffusion (DaSilva et al., 2025) demonstrated that diffusion models in the second regime can pro-
pose diverse, motif-plausible candidates scoring highly under chromatin predictors, using a U-Net
denoiser. Our work replaces this with a parameter-efficient DiT backbone and adds post-training
alignment to predictor objectives.
3 METHODS
3.1 DATA
We consider the problem of generating synthetic 200 bp DNA sequences intended to function as
regulatory elements that increase cell-type-specific activity under learned proxy predictors following
DaSilva et al. (2025). Specifically, we focus on designing regulatory elements that enhance the gene
activity in K562, HepG2, GM12878, and hECT0 cells. Starting with ENCODE DHS data which
identify DNase I hypersensitive sites (DHSs) that mark regions of open chromatin and regulatory
activity, we identify peaks of DNAseI activity to define cis-regulatory regions in each cell line.
Following DNA-Diffusion, we use a dataset with 12k samples from each of the 4 cell lines, ensuring
that the sequences of DNA do not repeat between the cells. In total, our dataset consists of 47,872
sequences.
3.2 MODEL FORMULATION AND PRELIMINARIES
We train a diffusion model to denoise corrupted continuous representations of DNA sequences fol-
lowing the standard DDPM protocol from Ho et al. (2020). Specifically, we use Adam (Kingma &
Ba, 2017) with learning rate2×10−4, bf16 mixed precision, and batch size1024. The diffusion
process uses100timesteps with a linear noise schedule fromβ start= 0.296toβ end= 0.25and
unconditional dropoutp uncond = 0.1for classifier-free guidance.
Our DiT (dim= 320, depth= 6,8heads) uses AdaLN-Zero conditioning with learned positional
embeddings. The4×200one-hot input is processed through a 2D CNN encoder (kernel size5)
that treats the nucleotide×position matrix as a spatial feature map, capturing local k-mer structure
before the transformer layers. Architecture and alternative input format ablations are reported in
subsection 4.4. The U-Net baseline follows the original DNA-Diffusion architecture (DaSilva et al.,
2025) withdim = 200and channel multipliers[1,2,4]. We train for a minimum of2,000epochs
with early stopping (patience10). At inference, we use classifier-free guidance with scalew= 2.0.
3.3 POST-TRAINING VIA REINFORCEMENT LEARNING/PREDICTOR-GUIDED FINETUNING
Our finetuning setup is RL-algorithm agnostic and simply modifies the inference setup and reward
signal. At each training iteration, we randomly sample a target cell type and condition both the
diffusion sampler and reward function on this cell. Candidate sequences are generated via classifier-
free guidance using the selected cell embedding, and rewards are computed from the corresponding
Enformer output track predicting the CAGE for that cell (Avsec et al., 2021a). Policy updates are
then performed using denoising diffusion policy optimization (DDPO) (Black et al., 2023). The
training loop is detailed in Appendix subsection A.3.
We consider two training scenarios. In thein situsetting, Enformer evaluates the generated DNA
embedded within the GATA1 locus, testing the model’s ability to produce sequences that interact
with distal genomic context. In theex situsetting, the enhancer is evaluated in isolation, requiring
the model to encode enhancer-specific structure directly within the 200 bp insert.
3.4 CROSS-VALIDATION
Finally, we verify that our model does not overfit to the Enformer model. Using an oracle for pre-
dicting HepG2 activity, we evaluate our conditional DNA generation compared to that of single-cell
diffusion model DRAKES (Wang et al., 2024). Notably, our dataset (with 12k HepG2 sequences)

rather to confirm that our generations exhibit a meaningful structural signal that generalizes to these
constraints.

Our DiT matches the best validation loss of the U-Net baseline within 13 epochs (∼60×fewer), and
ultimately converges 39% lower (0.023 vs. 0.037), as illustrated in Figure 1.
We note that a key concern with generative DNA models is memorization, in this context meaning
that the model produces near-copies of training sequences rather than novel regulatory candidates.
We evaluate this with two complementary analyses. BLAT alignment (Kent, 2002) queries each
generated sequence against the full training set for high-identity matches (≥20 bp,≥90% identity);
a high match rate indicates memorization. Motif JS distance scans all sequences for 879 transcription
factor (TF) binding motifs from JASPAR (Rauluseviciute et al., 2024) and compares their frequency
distribution s between generated and held-out test sequences via Jensen–Shannon divergence; low
JS distance indicates that the model has learned biologically realistic motif usage rather than copying
specific sequences.

We demonstrate in Figure 2 that the generation quality of our DiT matches prior DNA-Diffusion
baselines on motif recovery (JS distance) while exhibiting substantially less memorization: only
1.7% of generated sequences align to the training set via BLAT (Kent, 2002), compared to 5.3% for
the U-Net reported by DaSilva et al. (2025). We attribute this to the transformer’s global attention
mechanism, which avoids the fixed receptive fields of convolutional architectures.

4.2 REINFORCEMENTLEARNING
Utilizing our training methodology and DDPO, we find that we are able to increase the predicted
in-situ expression over 38x compared to the baseline model on average Table 1. Evaluation was
conducted across 250 sequences generated for each cell line. We present the best RL results here,
though a sweep of RL hyperparameters can be found in A.4. In Figure 3, we additionally see that
over 75 percent of all generations, across all cell types, have higher Enformer score than the baseline
median.
4.3 CROSS-VALIDATION
For validation, we compare our model to the reported values of the DRAKES model, which is
optimized for maximizing single-cell (HepG2) expression. Our model captures 70% (3.86) of the
5.6 predicted activity by DRAKES, suggesting the presence of a meaningful signal under these
constraints.
4.4 ALTERNATIVEMODELINGAPPROACHES
Positional embeddings without CNN input preprocessing.We trained DiT variants using a lin-
ear projection of the4×200one-hot input (no convolutional encoder) with either RoPE or learned
positional embeddings. Both converged to validation losses of 0.038–0.039, roughly 70% higher
than the CNN2D model’s 0.023, with the gap persisting across 2,000 epochs.
Interestingly, RoPE achieved comparable motif JS distances to CNN2D (between 0.20–0.21 vs.
0.21–0.22), while learned embeddings fared worse (0.24–0.25). RoPE’s relative-position awareness
partially compensates for lacking local inductive bias, but cannot fully replace the CNN encoder’s

k-mer feature extraction. This is consistent with the broader observation that transformers benefit
from convolutional stems for spatially structured inputs.
5 DISCUSSION ANDLIMITATIONS
Our results demonstrate that transformer-based diffusion models can substantially outperform U-
Net baselines for regulatory DNA generation, but only when equipped with appropriate inductive
biases. As our ablation (subsection 4.4) shows, the CNN encoder is essential: without it, validation
loss increases 70% regardless of positional embedding choice, confirming that transformers require
convolutional stems to capture local structure in spatially organized inputs.
The 38×improvement in predicted expression from DDPO finetuning is encouraging, but carries
important caveats. Indeed, post-hoc analysis of DDPO-finetuned generations reveals a distribution
shift: while memorization of training data remains low (3.0% BLAT), self-alignment rises to 92.8%
indicating that the policy converges to a narrow distribution. Enformer, while state-of-the-art, is an
imperfect proxy: optimized sequences may exploit model-specific biases rather than genuine regula-
tory logic. Our DRAKES comparison partially mitigates this concern by showing that improvements
transfer to an independent predictor and task, but the use of other validation models (BORZOI or
AlphaGenome) and wet-lab validation (e.g., MPRA assays) remains necessary to confirm functional
activity. Additionally, our 200 bp generation window cannot capture distal regulatory interactions,
and our balanced 12k-per-cell-type dataset is small relative to the full ENCODE dataset. Future
work will explore scaling to longer inserts, larger multi-cell datasets, and closed-loop experimental
validation.

structure.title: INTRODUCTION
structure.summary:
This partial document introduces a parameter-efficient Diffusion Transformer (DiT) model for generating synthetic regulatory DNA sequences. The model aims to address the challenge of designing short DNA sequences with specific regulatory effects for genetic modulation. Key contributions include:

*   **Continuous DiT for Regulatory Design:** A transformer-based diffusion model is developed to generate 200 bp regulatory elements. This model reportedly surpasses previous methods in efficiency, requiring significantly fewer training steps and parameters.
*   **RL Optimization for Enhanced Regulatory Activity:** The model is further fine-tuned using Reinforcement Learning (RL) with Enformer as a reward model. This process aims to improve predicted regulatory activity and accessibility.
*   **Validation and Verification:** The effectiveness of the RL fine-tuning is validated against DRAKES on an independent prediction task, confirming that the improvements reflect genuine regulatory signals rather than reward model overfitting.
*   **Comparison to Existing Methods:** The paper contrasts its approach with existing methods, highlighting the limitations of U-nets for modeling long-distance DNA interactions and the benefits of transformers in this context.
*   **Technical Details:** The model replaces the U-Net backbone of DNA-Diffusion with a transformer denoiser and incorporates a 2D CNN input encoder, which is shown to be crucial for performance.

structure.title: RELATEDWORKS
structure.summary:
This partial document describes a novel approach called "Continuous Diffusion Transformers for Designing Synthetic Regulatory Elements." The main points covered are:

*   **Introduction of a Parameter-Efficient Diffusion Transformer (DiT):** The paper proposes replacing the U-Net backbone in DNA-Diffusion with a transformer denoiser, enhanced by a 2D CNN input encoder. This aims to improve efficiency and performance in generating short DNA sequences (200 bp) with specific regulatory functions.
*   **Performance Improvements:** The proposed DiT model achieves faster convergence (60x fewer epochs) and a lower validation loss compared to the U-Net baseline. It also significantly reduces memorization of training data.
*   **Importance of the CNN Encoder:** Ablation studies highlight that the 2D CNN encoder is crucial for the model's performance, as its removal leads to a substantial increase in validation loss.
*   **Reinforcement Learning (RL) Finetuning:** The model is further improved through RL finetuning using Enformer as a reward model, leading to a significant increase in predicted regulatory activity.
*   **Validation Against Reward Model Overfitting:** Cross-validation against DRAKES on an independent prediction task confirms that the observed improvements reflect genuine regulatory signals rather than overfitting to the reward model.
*   **Motivation for Transformer Choice:** The paper argues that transformers are better suited than U-nets for modeling long-distance DNA interactions due to their ability to handle variable receptive fields.
*   **Contributions:** The key contributions are the development of a parameter-efficient Continuous DiT for regulatory design and its post-training optimization using RL.
*   **Data and Methodology:** The document details the dataset used (ENCODE DHS data from four cell lines), the diffusion model formulation (DDPM protocol, Adam optimizer, bf16 precision), the DiT architecture, and the RL finetuning setup (DDPO, Enformer as reward, in-situ and ex-situ training scenarios).
*   **Cross-Validation Strategy:** The paper outlines how they verify their model's performance by comparing it to DRAKES using an independent oracle for predicting HepG2 activity.

structure.title: METHODS
structure.summary:
This partial document describes a generative approach for creating synthetic DNA sequences that function as regulatory elements. The work builds upon previous diffusion model research (DNA-Diffusion) by replacing the U-Net denoiser with a parameter-efficient DiT backbone and incorporating post-training alignment to predictor objectives.

The main points covered are:

*   **Generative DNA Models:** Two regimes are discussed: large foundation models and small-insert, objective-driven generators. The focus is on the latter, specifically using diffusion models.
*   **Methodology:**
    *   **Data:** The dataset consists of 47,872 synthetic 200 bp DNA sequences designed to enhance gene activity in specific cell types (K562, HepG2, GM12878, hECT0), derived from ENCODE DHS data.
    *   **Model Formulation:** A diffusion model is trained using the DDPM protocol with specific Adam optimizer settings, mixed precision, batch size, and noise schedule. A DiT backbone is employed, with a 2D CNN encoder for initial processing.
    *   **Post-Training Finetuning:** A reinforcement learning approach (DDPO) is used to align generated sequences with predictor objectives (Enformer output for CAGE prediction). This finetuning is performed in both "in situ" (within a genomic locus) and "ex situ" (in isolation) settings.
*   **Cross-Validation:** The model's performance is validated against another diffusion model (DRAKES) to ensure it doesn't overfit to the Enformer predictor.

This partial document describes a generative approach for creating synthetic DNA sequences that function as regulatory elements. The work builds upon previous diffusion model research (DNA-Diffusion) by replacing the U-Net denoiser with a parameter-efficient DiT backbone and incorporating post-training alignment to predictor objectives.

The main points covered are:

*   **Generative DNA Models:** Two regimes are discussed: large foundation models and small-insert, objective-driven generators. The focus is on the latter, specifically using diffusion models.
*   **Methodology:**
    *   **Data:** The dataset consists of 47,872 synthetic 200 bp DNA sequences designed to enhance gene activity in specific cell types (K562, HepG2, GM12878, hECT0), derived from ENCODE DHS data.
    *   **Model Formulation:** A diffusion model is trained using the DDPM protocol with specific Adam optimizer settings, mixed precision, batch size, and noise schedule. A DiT backbone is employed, with a 2D CNN encoder for initial processing.
    *   **Post-Training Finetuning:** A reinforcement learning approach (DDPO) is used to align generated sequences with predictor objectives (Enformer output for CAGE prediction). This finetuning is performed in both "in situ" (within a genomic locus) and "ex situ" (in isolation) settings.
*   **Cross-Validation:** The model's performance is validated against another diffusion model (DRAKES) to ensure it doesn't overfit to the Enformer predictor.

*   **Cross-Validation:** Discusses verifying the model's generalization by comparing it to another model (DRAKES) using an oracle for HepG2 activity prediction, despite differences in dataset size and labeling.

    *   **Convergence:** Demonstrates that their DiT model converges faster and achieves a lower validation loss compared to the U-Net baseline.
    *   **Memorization Analysis:** Evaluates the tendency of the model to memorize training sequences using BLAT alignment and motif usage analysis (Motif JS distance). The DiT model shows substantially less memorization than the U-Net baseline.
    *   **Motif Recovery:** Shows that the DiT model matches prior baselines in recovering biologically realistic motif usage.

structure.title: EXPERIMENTS
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses experiments and results related to a generative DNA model, specifically a DiT (Diffusion Transformer) model, compared to a U-Net baseline. The main points covered are:

*   **Experimental Setup and Goal:** The comparison aims to assess the structural signal and generalization capabilities of the DiT model, rather than matching absolute performance, due to differences in training tasks and datasets with a DRAKES model.
*   **Generation Quality and Convergence:** The DiT model demonstrates faster convergence and achieves a significantly lower validation loss compared to the U-Net baseline, as illustrated by loss curves.
*   **Memorization Analysis:** The document addresses the concern of generative models memorizing training data. Two methods are used to evaluate this:
    *   **BLAT Alignment:** Measures the percentage of generated sequences that are near-copies of training sequences. The DiT model shows substantially less memorization than the U-Net baseline.
    *   **Motif JS Distance:** Assesses whether the model has learned biologically realistic motif usage by comparing the frequency distribution of transcription factor binding motifs between generated and held-out test sequences. The DiT model performs comparably to baselines on this metric.
*   **Attribution of Performance:** The improved memorization performance of the DiT model is attributed to its transformer's global attention mechanism, which overcomes the limitations of fixed receptive fields in convolutional architectures.

nodes.title: GENERATION QUALITY
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses experiments and validation of a generative DNA model, likely named "DiT" (Diffusion Transformer). Key points covered include:

*   **Generation Quality:** The DiT model demonstrates faster convergence and lower validation loss compared to a U-Net baseline. It also shows reduced memorization of training data, as measured by BLAT alignment, while maintaining comparable motif usage (JS distance) to prior DNA-Diffusion baselines.
*   **Reinforcement Learning:** The document highlights the use of a training methodology and DDPO (likely a reinforcement learning algorithm) to significantly increase predicted in-situ expression of generated regulatory sequences, with a majority of generations exceeding the baseline median Enformer score.
*   **Cross-Validation:** The model's performance is compared to the DRAKES model, showing that the DiT model captures a substantial portion of the predicted activity, indicating a meaningful structural signal.
*   **Alternative Modeling Approaches:** Experiments with different positional embedding strategies (RoPE and learned embeddings) without CNN input preprocessing are discussed, showing that while they can partially compensate for the lack of local inductive bias, they do not match the performance of the CNN-based approach.
*   **Comparison with DRAKES:** The document notes that the DRAKES model is trained on a different dataset (700k Enhancers) and task compared to their model, and the goal of comparison is to assess the generalization of structural signals rather than absolute performance.

nodes.title: REINFORCEMENTLEARNING
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses a machine learning model, likely for biological sequence generation, and its performance evaluation. Key points include:

*   **Model Performance Comparison:** A table (Table 1) presents activity scores predicted by the Enformer model for regulatory sequences generated by different models (DNA-Diffusion, CNN-DiT, CNN-DiT-DDPO) across various cell types (GM12878, HepG2, K562, hESCT0) and training modes (In-Situ, Ex-Situ). Bolded values indicate the best performance within a category.
*   **Reinforcement Learning (RL) Improvements:** Section 4.2 highlights that their training methodology and DDPO (likely a reinforcement learning algorithm) significantly increase predicted in-situ expression (over 38x compared to a baseline). Figure 3 visually supports this, showing a distribution of Enformer scores for generated sequences, with a majority exceeding the baseline median.
*   **Cross-Validation with DRAKES:** Section 4.3 compares their model's performance to the DRAKES model, noting that their model captures a substantial portion (70%) of the predicted activity by DRAKES, which is optimized for single-cell expression.
*   **Alternative Modeling Approaches:** Section 4.4 explores alternative modeling approaches, specifically DiT variants using positional embeddings without CNN input preprocessing. It compares the performance of RoPE (Rotary Positional Embeddings) and learned positional embeddings against a CNN2D model, noting differences in validation loss and motif JS distances. The section suggests that RoPE's relative-position awareness offers some benefits but doesn't fully replace the CNN encoder.

nodes.title: ALTERNATIVEMODELINGAPPROACHES
nodes.summary:
This document excerpt discusses a transformer-based diffusion model for regulatory DNA generation, presented at the Gen2Workshop at ICLR 2026. Key points include:

*   **Model Performance and Training:** The document presents a table (Table 1) comparing the performance of different models (DNA-Diffusion, CNN-DiT, CNN-DiT-DDPO) across various cell types (GM12878, HepG2, K562, hESCT0) and training modes (In-Situ, Ex-Situ). It highlights that CNN-DiT-DDPO with In-Situ training achieves the best median activity scores.
*   **Reinforcement Learning (RL) Improvement:** Section 4.2 details how reinforcement learning, specifically using DDPO, significantly increases predicted in-situ expression (over 38x compared to the baseline) and that a majority of generated sequences show higher Enformer scores than the baseline median (Figure 3).
*   **Cross-Validation:** Section 4.3 compares the model's performance to the DRAKES model, indicating that it captures a substantial portion (70%) of the predicted activity, suggesting a meaningful signal.
*   **Alternative Modeling Approaches:** Section 4.4 explores the impact of positional embeddings versus CNN input preprocessing in DiT variants. It finds that CNN input preprocessing is crucial for capturing local structure, even when using advanced positional embeddings like RoPE.
*   **Discussion and Limitations:** Section 5 summarizes that transformer-based diffusion models outperform U-Net baselines when equipped with appropriate inductive biases (like CNN encoders). It discusses the caveats of the DDPO finetuning, including potential distribution shifts and the limitations of Enformer as a proxy for true regulatory logic. The need for further validation using other predictors and wet-lab experiments is emphasized. Limitations regarding the generation window size and dataset size are also noted, with future work planned to address these.
*   **References:** A list of cited works is provided, covering topics like hyperparameter optimization, gene expression prediction, transcription factor binding, diffusion models, and regulatory code prediction.

structure.title: DISCUSSION ANDLIMITATIONS
structure.summary: This partial document discusses the use of transformer-based diffusion models for regulatory DNA generation, highlighting their outperformance compared to U-Net baselines when equipped with appropriate inductive biases. A key finding is the essential role of a CNN encoder for transformers to capture local structure in spatially organized inputs. The document also addresses the limitations of DDPO finetuning, including a distribution shift towards memorization and the imperfect nature of Enformer as a proxy for regulatory logic. It suggests the need for validation using independent predictors and wet-lab experiments. Future work is planned to address limitations in generation window size and dataset scale. The appendix details the dataset used, including cell lines and ENCODE accession numbers, and describes a hyperparameter sweep for DiT models, identifying optimal configurations and factors that negatively impact performance.

nodes.title: RL ALGORITHMSPECIFICS
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes the experimental setup and results for a diffusion model applied to cell-specific regulatory design. It details hyperparameter tuning for RL algorithms, specifically focusing on DDPO, and compares different model configurations, including a U-Net baseline and a DiT CNN2D model. Key aspects covered include:

*   **Dataset and Hyperparameter Tuning:** The document mentions issues with dataset size, timesteps, and beta end values affecting performance. It highlights the selection of a best-performing trial configuration (Trial 14) for the DiT architecture.
*   **RL Algorithm Specifics:** An algorithm (Algorithm 1) for Task-Conditioned Diffusion RL for Cell-Specific Regulatory Design is presented, outlining the steps involving a diffusion policy, a frozen proxy predictor (Enformer), and the DDPO objective.
*   **RL Algorithm Hyperparameters:** Specific hyperparameters for DDPO, including learning rate and PPO epochs, are discussed, along with the chosen best configuration. Other RL algorithms like SDPO and GRPO were considered but found to be less effective.
*   **Model Configurations:** A comparison table (Table 3) details the architecture and training configurations of a U-Net baseline (DNA-Diffusion) and the proposed DiT CNN2D model. This includes parameters like backbone, input encoding, hidden dimensions, depth, attention heads, diffusion timesteps, noise schedules, and beta values. The DiT CNN2D model achieved a better validation loss.
